N361873  
June 17, 2026
  OT:RR:NC:N1:102  
CATEGORY: Origin  Monique Corona  Professional Plumbing Group Inc.  51 Lacrue Avenue  Glen Mills, PA 19382  RE:  The country of origin of a sump pump  Dear Ms. Corona:  In your letter dated May 28, 2026, you requested a country of origin ruling on a sump pump.  The product at issue is a Sump Pump, part number 80745. The submersible pump is commonly installed in  basements of homes and buildings to automatically remove accumulated water to prevent flooding. The  pump features a power cord and a float switch and consists of a stainless-steel body that encases an impeller  and a power motor.  With respect to origin, the final assembly of the pump occurs in Thailand using components from Thailand  and China. Prior to the final assembly, the motor assembly occurs in Thailand. This process begins by  attaching an O-ring, a wire bushing, a tapping screw, a lock washer, a grounding lead, and a spring washer to   the top of a motor housing from China. Afterwards, the rotor and stator, both from Thailand, are assembled  into the motor housing and enclosed using screws. Once complete, the motor is lubricated.  The final assembly begins by threading and securing a power cord from Thailand through a hole on the top of  the main housing from Thailand. Afterwards, a capacitor from China, a cable sheath from China, a cable  retainer from Thailand, and a block from Thailand are secured in place using tapping screws. In the next step,  a main pump housing assembly from Thailand is installed onto a motor assembly and screwed in place using   rings, bearings, and washers. The process continues by placing an impeller from China onto the motor-pump  subassembly. Lastly, a floating switch from Thailand is affixed onto the side of the main pump housing.  Various tests and inspections are completed during the assembly process.  When determining the country of origin for purposes of applying current trade remedies under Section 301  and additional duties, the substantial transformation analysis is applicable. See, e.g., Headquarters Ruling  Letter H301619, dated November 6, 2018. The test for determining whether a substantial transformation will  occur is whether an article emerges from a process with a new name, character, or use different from that 

possessed by the article prior to processing. See Texas Instruments Inc. v. United States, 681 F.2d 778  (C.C.P.A. 1982). This determination is based on the totality of the evidence. See National Hand Tool Corp. v.  United States, 16 C.I.T. 308 (1992), aff’d, 989 F.2d 1201 (Fed. Cir. 1993).  The final assembly processes conducted in Thailand, which merely involve placing and screwing  components, are considered simple and do not impart a substantial transformation. Since these operations do  not meet the criteria for substantial transformation, CBP's determination of origin shifts to the essential  component, which CBP has consistently deemed to be the motor for most pumps and pump assemblies. This  position is supported by previous rulings, including New York Ruling Letters N347899, dated May 2, 2025,  and N316993, dated February 12, 2021. Accordingly, as the motor originates in Thailand, the country of  origin for the subject sump pump is Thailand.  The holding set forth above applies only to the specific factual situation and merchandise description as  identified in the ruling request. This position is clearly set forth in Title 19, Code of Federal Regulations  (CFR), Section 177.9(b)(1). This section states that a ruling letter is issued on the assumption that all of the  information furnished in the ruling letter, whether directly, by reference, or by implication, is accurate and  complete in every material respect. In the event that the facts are modified in any way, or if the goods do not  conform to these facts at time of importation, you should bring this to the attention of U.S. Customs and  Border Protection (CBP) and submit a request for a new ruling in accordance with 19 CFR 177.2.  Additionally, we note that the material facts described in the foregoing ruling may be subject to periodic  verification by CBP.  This ruling is being issued under the provisions of Part 177 of the Customs and Border Protection  Regulations (19 C.F.R. 177).  A copy of the ruling or the control number indicated above should be provided with the entry documents  filed at the time this merchandise is imported. If you have any questions regarding the ruling, please contact  National Import Specialist Sandra Martinez at sandra.martinez@cbp.dhs.gov.  
Sincerely,
  (for)  James P. Forkan  Director  National Commodity Specialist Division
